A survey-weighted multivariate Linear Probability Model (LPM) Oaxaca-Blinder decomposition was applied to a complete-case cohort (N=16,179) to partition the prevalence change into population-level compositional shifts (endowments) and behavioral changes (coefficients). Results National Caesarean section prevalence surged by 32.47 percentage points, rising from 19.48% in 2012 to 36.05% in 2019 and 51.95% in 2025 (p<0.001). Surgical delivery multiplied over sixfold among the poorest wealth quintile (5.53% to 34.37%), rose by 34.83 percentage points among rural mothers (15.66% to 50.49%), and reached 85.12% within private facilities. Multivariate decomposition demonstrated that 87.77% of the overall increase was attributable to compositional shifts rather than behavioral factors (12.23%). The sharp reduction in pregnancies receiving zero ANC visits (35.52% to 8.12%) independently drove 49.04% of the surge, while increased utilization of private clinics and NGOs (18.20% to 54.36%) explained 43.39%. Conversely, biological indications such as fetal macrosomia contributed less than 1%. Conclusions The unprecedented escalation of Caesarean sections in Bangladesh represents a profound pattern of systemic over-medicalization that is independent of baseline clinical risk. The surge is overwhelmingly structural, driven by the disproportionate concentration of deliveries within the commercialized private healthcare sector and supplier-induced demand following integration into formal clinical pathways. Reversing this trajectory necessitates immediate regulatory intervention, specifically the mandate of clinical auditing frameworks such as the Robson classification, to decouple financial incentives from obstetric decision-making in private facilities.

Title: Integrating 16S and 18S sequencing reveals coupled prokaryotic and eukaryotic relationships in drinking water biofilms
Authors: Caligaris, L.; Hammes, F.; Cristino, S.; Gabrielli, M.
Abstract: Drinking water biofilms host diverse communities spanning all realms of life. However, despite the known interactions between opportunistic pathogens and microbial eukaryotes such as amoebae, most studies focus only on the prokaryotic populations in these systems. As a result, the degree to which microbial eukaryotes shape biofilm communities and the persistence of opportunistic waterborne pathogens, such as Legionella spp. is still largely unknown. Here we leveraged a set of 128 non-disinfected drinking water shower hose biofilms collected across Switzerland to characterize both communities and quantify eukaryotes' role in shaping prokaryotic communities and Legionella persistence. We found both communities to present a conserved set of core taxa dominated by oligotrophic bacterial families and amoebae. The prevalence of taxa was mainly driven by the phylogenetic diversity among their sequence variants rather than their number alone. We detected prokaryotic and eukaryotic communities to show similar patterns in their richness and composition, influencing each other more than abiotic building-level factors. Legionellaceae bacteria were detected in 82% of samples presenting a diversity extending known reference species and no clear dominant taxa. Legionellaceae richness did not correlate with the richness of known amoebal hosts, but rather other amoebae, indicating that eukaryotic taxa relevant for Legionella persistence extend beyond the classically described hosts. These findings highlight the importance of integrating the eukaryotic communities to understand the microbial ecology in drinking water biofilms and recognize the conditions which allow opportunistic waterborne pathogens such as Legionella to persist.

Title: Assessing HIV vulnerability among young women in South Africa: A comparison of three risk assessment tools
Authors: Dubazana, S. E.; Hendrickson, C.; Greener, R.; Shahmanesh, M.; Govindasamy, D.; Musenge, E.; Miot, J.; Long, L.
Abstract: Background: Young women in sub-Saharan Africa remain disproportionately affected by HIV. However, self-perceived HIV risk may not align with reported sexual behaviours or other dimensions of risk. Behavioural measures, such as the Balloon Analogue Risk Task (BART), may capture risk-taking propensity not reflected in conventional self-report measures. We compared self-perceived HIV risk, behaviour-based HIV risk, and behavioural risk-taking propensity among young women in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Methods: We conducted a cross-sectional survey between July and November 2025 among self-reported HIV-negative women aged 18-30 years in KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa. Self-perceived HIV risk was assessed using the Perceived Risk of HIV Scale (PRHS), behaviour-based HIV risk using the Vaginal and Oral Interventions to Control the Epidemic (VOICE) Risk Score, and behavioural risk-taking propensity using BART. Spearman's rank correlation coefficients were used to examine convergence between the three measures. Results: Among 250 participants, median age was 22 years (IQR 20-25), all identified as Black, and 53.6% were attending school or college. Overall, 42.0% were classified as high risk by VOICE, 6.0% by PRHS, and 33.1% of participants with complete BART data were in the highest tertile of risk-taking propensity. Mean age differed across VOICE categories (p = 0.036), but not PRHS (p = 0.111) or BART categories (p = 0.698). PRHS categories were associated with anal intercourse, oral intercourse, consistent condom use, ever having sold sex, and age-disparate partnerships (all p < 0.05). VOICE categories were not significantly associated with the assessed sexual behaviours, while BART categories were associated with vaginal intercourse in the past month (p = 0.042). Correlations between PRHS, VOICE, and BART were weak and non-significant (Spearman's rho = 0.001-0.057; all p > 0.05). Conclusions: Self-perceived HIV risk, behaviour-based HIV risk, and behavioural risk-taking propensity showed limited convergence in this sample. The measures also differed in their associations with participant characteristics and reported sexual behaviours, suggesting that they capture distinct dimensions of risk. Further research should investigate whether integrating behavioural measures with conventional self-report assessments improves understanding of HIV vulnerability and informs prevention approaches tailored to young women.

Title: Risk Omission and Limited Disclosure in Dietary Supplement Promotion by Social Media Influencers
Authors: Engel, E.; Karsay, K.; Moeri, M.; Vos, I.; Friemel, T.; Nickel, B.; Heiss, R.
Abstract: Importance: Dietary supplements carry risks including adverse effects, drug interactions, and contamination-related harms, yet are frequently marketed without premarket requirements for efficacy or safety. Social media influencers have become a primary source through which people encounter and make decisions about supplements, but whether they communicate clinically relevant risks alongside claimed benefits remains unclear. Objective: To investigate how dietary supplements are presented by Instagram influencers, focusing on supplement types, advertising disclosure, persuasive strategies, and communication of benefits and harms. Design, Setting, and Participants: Cross-sectional content analysis of 1,120 dietary supplement presentations in 727 Instagram posts by 84 influencer accounts identified through audience-centered purposive sampling from two independent youth-focused studies in Switzerland and Austria. Main Outcomes and Measures: Main outcomes were supplement types, overall tone, advertising disclosure, persuasive strategies, and communication of benefits and harms, all summarized descriptively. Logistic regression with cluster-robust standard errors assessed whether influencer type or supplement category influenced presentation characteristics. Results: Of 1,120 supplement presentations, 1092 (97.5%) were promotional in tone, 1088 (97.1%) involved advertising, but disclosure was absent in 802 advertisements (73.7%). Protein (463 [41.3%]), caffeine (156 [13.9%]), creatine (71 [6.3%]), and (multi-)vitamins (67 [6.0%]) were the most frequently identified ingredients. Benefits were mentioned in 269 presentations (24.0%); harms in only 26 (2.3%), mostly framing supplements as unnecessary or cautioning about side effects. No presentation mentioned drug interactions, contamination risks, or contraindications. Benefit claims were more common in presentations featuring micronutrient and miscellaneous ingredient supplements, and less common in presentations featuring sport nutrition supplements. Influencers with health credentials were more likely to include evidence cues than nonprofessionals (adjusted OR, 81.05; 95% CI, 13.76-477.44); associations with tone and personal experience narratives were not robust to adjustment. Conclusions and Relevance: Influencer presentation of supplements was highly commercialized, largely undisclosed, and characterized by a substantial imbalance between benefit and risk communication. The absence of clinically relevant risk information suggests that individuals relying on such content are unlikely to receive balanced safety information, underscoring the need for stronger regulation and proactive clinician inquiry about supplement use.

Title: Biological age uncertainty reveals discordant aging and predicts human healthspan
Authors: Li, Y.; Feng, G.; Yan, S.; Huang, Q.; Jiang, J.; Pei, Z.; Tay, L. X.; Li, K.; Pan, Z.; Yuan, Z.; Gao, L.; Ji, J. S.; Ke, L.; Gu, K.; Di, Q.
Abstract: Biological aging clocks typically summarize complex biological profiles as a single age estimate, yet how uncertain these estimates are and whether this uncertainty represents a distinct, biologically meaningful dimension of human aging remain unclear. Here, we develop a probabilistic framework across nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) metabolomic, plasma proteomic and routine blood test (RBT) profiles in more than 450,000 UK Biobank participants to derive biological age gap (BAG) and biological age uncertainty (BAU) from the mean and width of predicted-age distributions. BAU was weakly correlated with BAG and increased with age-signal disagreement across individual molecules and organs, linking uncertainty to discordant aging across biological systems. Higher BAU predicted mortality, loss of healthspan and multimorbidity independently of BAG, with mortality hazard ratios of 1.24 (95% CI, 1.23-1.26) and 1.40 (95% CI, 1.37-1.43) per standard deviation for NMR- and proteomic-derived BAU, respectively. Adding BAU to conventional clinical models improved 10-year risk discrimination; moreover, longitudinal increases in NMR-derived BAU tracked subsequent health decline, and mortality associations were replicated using RBT-derived BAU across three independent external cohorts. Multi-omics and physiological analyses linked BAU to inflammation, metabolic dysregulation and tissue remodeling beyond BAG. Genetic analyses further revealed overlapping but distinct architectures of BAU and BAG, with BAU showing stronger genetic correlations with frailty and cardiometabolic diseases, and tissue and functional mapping implicating hepatic, immune and lipid-metabolic processes. This study establishes a framework for characterizing biological age through both its mean deviation and uncertainty, defining BAU as an independent dimension of human aging that links discordant aging to future healthspan.

Title: Baseline Physical Activity Guideline Attainment and Mortality Across Cardiovascular-Kidney-Metabolic Syndrome Stages
Authors: Luo, X.; Wang, Y.; Zhou, W.; Yu, F.; Sun, J.; Xiang, K.-F.; Wang, F.; Yuan, Z.; Bao, J.; Zhang, S.; Zheng, Y.; Wu, F.
Abstract: Background The 2023 American Heart Association cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) staging framework supports risk stratification, but evidence on guideline-level physical activity across stages remains limited. Methods We emulated a target-trial protocol using NHANES 2007-2018 and National Death Index linkage through December 31, 2019. Adults aged 20 to 79 years with CKM stages 1 to 4, estimated glomerular filtration rate of at least 15 mL/min/1.73 m2, complete activity data, no cancer history, and eligible follow-up were included. Baseline activity was classified as meeting or not meeting the guideline. Within-stage propensity-score weights were used in weighted Cox models. All-cause and cardiovascular mortality were the primary and secondary outcomes; 5-year risks used weighted survival curves, with competing-risk cumulative incidence also estimated for cardiovascular mortality. Results Among 19,654 participants, 1,190 all-cause deaths occurred during 134,037 person-years. Baseline attainment was associated with lower all-cause mortality overall (HR, 0.774; 95% CI, 0.675-0.888). Stage-specific HRs were 1.030, 0.803, 0.642, and 0.727 for stages 1 to 4, respectively; estimates were nonmonotonic. Five-year risk differences were +0.040, -0.830, -1.790, and -3.840 percentage points; only the stage 4 interval excluded the null. Cardiovascular mortality showed a similar overall cause-specific association (HR, 0.707; 95% CI, 0.547-0.914). Conclusions Observed baseline guideline attainment was associated with mortality in this observational target-trial emulation. The findings are consistent with current physical activity recommendations but do not estimate the effect of an activity-promotion intervention; prospective trials are needed to establish clinical benefit.

Title: Non-contact fingertip video to differentiate dengue haemorrhagic fever in plasma leakage from dengue fever: A prospective proof-of-concept cohort study
Authors: Perera, M. H. M. T. S.; Manamperi, S. T.; Athukorala, S. A. A. J. M.; Wijayawardhana, K. W. S. M.; Wimalasundera, A. R.; Arasaratnam, S.; Prathapa, D. M. J.; Kularathne, Y.
Abstract: Most patients with dengue recover without intervention, but a minority develop plasma leakage that threatens the circulation, and differentiating them is the central problem in dengue care. Platelet count is the marker in routine serial use and is itself one of the four defining criteria of dengue haemorrhagic fever (DHF), so thrombocytopenia in dengue fever (DF) can overlap with DHF on the very marker used to distinguish them. We asked whether a non-contact optical signal carries discriminative information beyond platelet count. We conducted a prospective observational cohort study at a national dengue referral centre. All DHF recordings were obtained at or after plasma-leakage onset, so the analysis compares established clinical states rather than pre-leakage risk. Serial non-contact fingertip videos were recorded with contemporaneous clinical and haematological measurements. In a held-out set of 50 recordings (20 DHF, 30 DF), video-derived probability separated the groups with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.963 (95% CI 0.918-1.000; 0.957 averaged across eight architectures). In the 49 recordings with a platelet count, the video AUC was 0.961 against 0.888 for platelet count (difference 0.074, p = 0.19). In exploratory analyses the video added information to platelet count (likelihood-ratio p < 0.001), showed no significant within-group correlation with platelet count, and retained an AUC of 0.970 against thrombocytopenic DF, where platelet count fell to 0.759. Bedside pulse rate, body temperature and haematocrit did not separate the groups and were unrelated to the video score. A ~30-second fingertip video separated DHF in plasma leakage from DF in this test set, and exploratory analyses suggest it carries information beyond platelet count. These findings are proof of concept from single-centre internal validation, not evidence of pre-leakage prediction; prospective pre-leakage studies and external validation are needed to establish whether the signal can support earlier risk stratification.

Title: Antimicrobial resistance patterns among urinary isolates from long-term care residents in Canada: findings from an AMRNet pilot
Authors: Yadav, C.; Amaratunga, K.; Bharat, A.; Afra, K.; Brown, K. A.; Chato, C.; Daneman, N.; Langford, B.; McDonald, G.; Ding, X.; Norgaard, C.; Faires, M.; Hoang, L.; Kibsey, P.; Lee, E.; Mak, A.; Minion, J.; Daley, P.; Rudnick, W.
Abstract: Background: Antimicrobial resistance is a growing concern in long-term care facilities (LTCs), where residents are often older, have chronic health conditions, and are frequently prescribed antimicrobials. Historically, antimicrobial resistance data from Canadian LTCs have been limited. This study explores the use of lab-based surveillance data from the Public Health Agency of Canada's AMRNet program to describe antimicrobial resistance in LTCs. Methods: Antimicrobial susceptibility data for clinical bacterial specimens were submitted from public and private laboratories across Canada. Where feasible, LTC patients were identified by submitting jurisdictions. Data on urinary isolates from identified LTC patients were analysed using the first isolate per patient per species per calendar year. The data were described by distribution of age group, sex, species and antimicrobial susceptibility. Antimicrobials were classified by the World Health Organization's 'Access, Watch and Reserve' (AWaRe) framework and a weighted-incidence syndromic combination antibiogram was constructed. As part of AMRNet program development, in some jurisdictions, only certain specimen types or organisms were submitted. Not all jurisdictions participated every year. Due to privacy precautions, some values rely on estimations. Results: From 2016-2024, AMRNet received data on 216,524 isolates from five provinces (BC, NL, ON, PEI, SK). Most isolates (98%) were from patients aged >=60, with those >=80 years representing 80%; females predominated across all age groups. Urine represented >99% of submitted data. The most common organisms identified from urinary isolates were Escherichia coli (51%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (14%) and Proteus mirabilis (12%). Non susceptibility varied across organisms: E. coli demonstrated higher non-susceptibility to several commonly used agents including fluoroquinolones (44%) and third generation cephalosporins (18%) while K. pneumoniae displayed high non-susceptibility to nitrofurantoin (56%). Among P. mirabilis, 26% were non susceptible to ciprofloxacin. Aminoglycoside and carbapenem resistance were low. When antimicrobials were grouped by WHO AWaRe categories, more than half of E. coli isolates were non-susceptible to at least one Watch antimicrobial. Interpretation: AMRNet lab-based surveillance data can help describe national AMR patterns among LTC residents. Although limitations exist and identifying LTC patients in lab-based datasets can be challenging in some jurisdictions, these data provide a feasible and cost-effective means of tracking national resistance trends among an at-risk population.

Title: The relation of a blood DNA methylation score with six-year depression course and risk factors
Authors: Klose, D.; Milaneschi, Y.; Boks, M. P. M.; van der Wee, N. J. A.; Lakerveld, J.; Vinkers, C.; Penninx, B. W. J. H.; Han, L. K. M.
Abstract: Background: DNA methylation (DNAm) signatures of major depressive disorder (MDD) may be related to psychosocial, environmental, biological, and lifestyle risks. We tested a blood-based DNAm depression score (MD-MS) based on an existing EWAS (N = 24,754) in N = 731 individuals for predicting 8 clinical and 16 MDD risk factors and whether different MDD trajectories mapped to changes in MD-MS over six years. Methods: We calculated the MD-MS based on the top 15 strongest, epigenome-wide significant depression associated sites from the largest EWAS to date in EPICv2-profiled blood samples from N = 366 NESDA participants at baseline and N = 365 at six-year follow-up (FU6). Sixty percent of participants obtained a lifetime MDD diagnosis before or during the study timeframe. Linear mixed effect models were used for all analyses. Results: The MD-MS was elevated in lifetime MDD vs. controls ({beta}=0.137, p=0.012). Lower social activity ({beta}=0.051, p=0.043), CRP ({beta}=0.068, p=0.006), triglycerides ({beta}=0.055, p=0.036) and fasting glucose ({beta}=0.059, p=0.025) showed positive associations with MD-MS, while higher neighborhood air pollution levels showed a negative association ({beta}=-0.054, p=0.031). Adjustment for psychosocial variables (social activity, childhood trauma, partner status) attenuated the MD-MS association with lifetime MDD by 17.5% ({beta}=0.114, p=0.051). Longitudinally, individuals with chronic MDD exhibited consistently higher MD-MS compared to controls ({beta} = 0.295, p = 0.001). Conclusions: The MD-MS captures an epigenetic signature of lifetime exposure to MDD. The significant influences of psychosocial and biological factors on this association, although of limited effect size, warrant further research on potentially actionable mechanisms against aberrant depression-related DNAm patterns.

Title: Sexual identity and seeking mental healthcare in young adults: A national cohort study
Authors: Khanolkar, A.; Camp, J.; Hill, A.; Curcin, V.; Becares, L.
Abstract: Aim: Most evidence on sexual minority health focuses on quantifying mental health inequalities with limited evidence on differences in accessing and receiving mental healthcare. This study examined associations between sexual identity and self-reported seeking and receiving mental healthcare in young adults from a population-based cohort study. Methods: 12,782 individuals (22% LGBQ+) aged 23 from the UK wide Millennium Cohort Study. Associations between sexual identity (heterosexual [reference category], mainly heterosexual, gay/lesbian and other sexual identities[LGBQ+]) assessed at age 17 and seeking mental healthcare were examined using multivariable logistic regression with sequential adjustment for sociodemographic factors (sex/ethnicity/SES), past (ages 14-17) and current (age 23) mental health, victimisation, loneliness and social support. Associations between sexual identity and receiving mental healthcare at age 23 was examined using multivariable logistic regression among those who sought help. Predicted probabilities were estimated from logistic models for interpretation. Results: All LGBQ+ groups had higher odds of seeking mental healthcare than heterosexuals. In the minimally-adjusted model, predicted probability of seeking care was lowest for heterosexual (24%), highest for bisexual (45%) and gay/lesbian individuals (49%). These significant differences attenuated but persisted in fully adjusted models, narrowing the probability gap between heterosexual and LGBQ+ groups from 25% to 10%. Furthermore, mental health history independently predicted help-seeking behaviour at age 23 among heterosexuals; but not in LGBQ+ groups. Among individuals seeking support, LGBQ+ groups had higher odds of receiving care than heterosexual peers, with highest baseline probabilities observed in the other sexual identity group (35% vs 15%). These differences remained largely unchanged after adjustment. Conclusion: LGBQ+ groups face substantial disparities, demonstrating significantly higher odds of both seeking and receiving mental healthcare than heterosexual peers. Crucially, the elevated rates of receiving care persist after full adjustment, indicating that these inequalities remain largely independent of downstream mediators and mental health history.

Title: Sacral nerve stimulation is more efficient in facilitating pelvic floor responses than pudendal nerve stimulation
Authors: Nissen, M. S.; Moore, M. B.; Chen, P.-J.; Vandegrift, B.; Gupta, P.; Bruns, T. M.
Abstract: Introduction: Sacral neuromodulation (SNM) is a third line treatment for pelvic organ dysfunction. Pudendal nerve stimulation (PNS) uses SNM electrode leads in an off-label fashion to also treat pelvic dysfunction. Differences in how stimulation of these two nerve targets activates the urethra and external anal sphincter (EAS) may provide insights into the mechanisms of these therapies. Materials and Methods: During SNM lead implant surgeries, needle electrodes and a high-resolution manometry catheter were used to record EAS electromyography (EMG) and multi-segment urethra pressure, respectively. Intra-operative sacral nerve stimulation (SNS) was performed, and EMG and pressure data were analyzed to examine relationships between the responses and stimulation. Pressure data was then compared to previously collected PNS-evoked responses. Results: Nine participants had data recorded during a SNM lead implant surgery. The applied current threshold to activate the urethra was significantly higher than visual motor threshold (VMT; p = 0.04). The EAS threshold was higher but not significantly different from VMT (p = 0.06). Maximum urethra pressure changes during SNS were not different from PNS driven changes (p = 0.09). Current amplitudes required to elicit maximum changes in urethra pressure were lower for SNS than PNS (p = 0.01) and the maximum change in urethra pressure per mA of applied stimulation was higher for SNS than PNS (p = 0.005). Conclusion: This is the first work to compare muscle recruitment between SNS and PNS in humans. SNS has greater pelvic floor recruitment per step in current than PNS. Typical SNM leads are closer to the nerve target, which may contribute to this effect.

Title: Rapid direct-from-urine growth detection to triage culture-negative urine: a prospective diagnostic accuracy study of a two-tube nitrate-reduction and bromothymol blue assay (SIBURI/SIBURI+)
Authors: Naik, R. R.; Naik, L. S.; Naik, P.; Paryekar, R. E.; Estibeiro, A. S.
Abstract: Objectives: Urine culture takes 24 to 72 h to report, and most specimens are culture-negative. We evaluated whether a 6-h direct-from-urine growth-detection assay can identify culture-negative specimens.Methods: In a prospective single-centre study at Goa Medical College, 145 consecutive urine specimens from patients with suspected urinary tract infection (UTI) were tested in parallel. Urine (50 uL) was added to SIBURI (nitrate-reduction broth, developed with Griess reagent) and SIBURI+ (Luria-Bertani broth with bromothymol blue) and incubated for 6 h at 37 C. Any visible colour change against an uninoculated blank was scored growth-positive. The reference standard was quantitative culture (greater than or equal to 10^5 CFU/mL of a single organism). Twenty-five specimens reported as contaminated, SCC or with greater than or equal to 3 organisms were excluded. Accuracy was estimated with exact 95 percent confidence intervals. A cell-free nitrite series and ATCC Escherichia coli and Klebsiella pneumoniae dilution series characterised the colour response.Results: Of 120 analysed specimens, 41 (34.2 percent) were culture-positive. Sensitivity was 92.7 percent (95 percent CI 80.1 to 98.5), specificity 92.4 percent (84.2 to 97.2), negative predictive value (NPV) 96.1 percent (88.9 to 99.2) and positive predictive value 86.4 percent (72.6 to 94.8). SIBURI alone detected 29 of 41 culture-positive specimens (70.7 percent); nine (enterococci, streptococcus, Acinetobacter, Candida and two unspecified) were detected only by SIBURI+. Classifying the excluded specimens as culture-positive gave a sensitivity of 93.9 percent and an NPV of 94.8 percent; classifying them as culture-negative lowered specificity to 71.2 percent. The colour response was biphasic: pink to red from 10 uM to 1 mM nitrite, and yellow above 1.5 mM.Conclusions: In this single-centre study, a two-tube 6-h assay showed good accuracy against culture, but the lower confidence limits (sensitivity 80.1 percent, NPV 88.9 percent) do not yet support omitting culture after a negative result. Positive results need culture confirmation, and larger multicentre validation is required.

Title: Serum Vitamin D Levels do not Affect Susceptibility to EBV Infection. A Mendelian Randomization Study.
Authors: Stanley, J.; Hamilton, F.; Davey Smith, G.
Abstract: Abstract Introduction: Epstein-Barr virus (EBV) infection and low serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D (25OHD) levels are strongly associated with multiple sclerosis (MS). We investigated whether genetically proxied serum vitamin D levels are causally linked to EBV infection, assessed by serology and detectable EBV DNA, using Mendelian randomisation (MR). Methods: We conducted two-sample cis-MR using genetic instruments associated with serum 25OHD concentrations, restricted to variants near genes implicated in vitamin D metabolism. Outcomes included EBV seropositivity, antibody responses to four EBV antigens, detectable EBV DNA in blood and saliva, and MS case status as a positive control. Results: Genetically proxied vitamin D levels had no clear effect on EBV seropositivity (odds ratio per standard deviation (SD) increase in rank-based inverse-normal transformation (RINT) 25OHD: 1.76, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.83-3.73) or antibody responses to EBV antigens. No significant associations were observed with detectable EBV DNA in blood (beta 0.02, 95% CI -0.004 to 0.04) or saliva (beta 0.02, 95% CI -0.23 to 0.26). In contrast, genetically proxied vitamin D levels were associated with reduced MS risk (odds ratio per SD increase in RINT 25OHD 0.67, 95% CI 0.54-0.84). Discussion: We found no clear evidence that genetically proxied vitamin D levels causally influence EBV serological responses or detectable EBV DNA in blood or saliva. The protective association with MS supports previous genetic evidence. These findings suggest that vitamin D and EBV may influence MS risk through distinct pathways, although effects specific to early-life vitamin D exposure remain possible.

Title: Identifying shared and parasite-specific determinants of Plasmodium falciparum and Schistosoma mansoni co-infection in a large-scale community-based study in rural Uganda
Authors: Lang, M. M.; Tuhaise, V.; Asiimwe, E.; Bogere, R.; Mohamed, A.; Isma, B.; Batte, J. D.; Nabatte, B.; Kabatereine, N. B.; Donnelly, C. A.; Chami, G. F.
Abstract: Malaria and schistosomiasis are co-endemic across much of sub-Saharan Africa, yet it remains unclear whether co-infections reflect shared risk factors, unexplained biological determinants, or chance co-occurrence. We analysed data collected at recruitment from 4290 individuals aged 5-90 years across 52 villages in rural Uganda within the SchistoTrack cohort. A bivariate copula model was developed to separate shared and disease-specific associations from residual dependence. Prevalence was 41.47% for Schistosoma mansoni, 41.19% for Plasmodium falciparum, and 18.51% for co-infection. Prevalence overlapped in school-aged children with co-infection prevalence peaking at 13 years. Greater distance to a government health centre was the strongest shared determinant, apart from age, male gender and living in western districts, increasing the risk of both. Local water ecology influenced each pathogen in opposing directions. Fishing was associated with higher S. mansoni and co-infection risks, but not P. falciparum risk. A modelled scenario combining household drinking-water treatment, handwashing facilities and protected water sources with cessation of freshwater contact reduced co-infection prevalence by 32%. Our findings support integrated control around shared demographics and limited healthcare access and household water infrastructure, while highlighting the need for non-integrated approaches for ecological interventions aiming to reduce parasite-specific transmission determinants.

Title: Dermal macrophages acquire a TREM2-anchored profibrotic state in antiphospholipid syndrome that is reflected in the circulation
Authors: Shen, Y.; Liang, W.; Li, Q.; Madison, J. A.; Jing, R.; Kaza, N.; Chong, E.; Bogle, R.; Yalavarthi, S.; Sarosh, C.; Tambralli, A.; Zuo, Y.; Gudjonsson, J. E.; Shi, H.; Tsou, P.-S.; Tsoi, L. C.; Knight, J. S.
Abstract: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a systemic autoimmune disease best known for thrombosis and obstetric morbidity. APS is sometimes also characterized by chronic microvascular disease, which can impair renal and other organ function. Skin offers an accessible window into the tissue mechanisms underlying such manifestations. Our previous single-cell analysis of skin biopsies from three patients with established microvascular disease focused on dermal endothelial cells and implicated a Hippo-YAP1-CCN2 axis in vascular pathology. Here, we expanded single-cell profiling to dermal tissue from 30 patients with primary APS and 14 age- and sex-matched healthy controls to characterize different tissue-resident cell states and their intercellular communication networks. Cellular composition was largely preserved. Disease-associated differences were centered on myeloid transcriptional states and predicted interactions with stromal cells. Dermal myeloid cells acquired a TREM2-anchored, lipid-associated program characterized by increased expression of genes involved in lipid handling and lysosomal function. These TREM2 macrophages were the major predicted source of profibrotic osteopontin and target of stromal apolipoprotein E signaling. Expression of this dermal program correlated positively with plasma soluble TREM2 and osteopontin, and all three measures correlated inversely with estimated glomerular filtration rate. Furthermore, soluble TREM2 was higher in APS patients with suspected or established nephropathy than in those without nephropathy. Together, these findings identify a tissue macrophage program in primary APS that is reflected in the circulation and associated with renal involvement, suggesting a role for macrophage-stromal interactions in chronic microvascular disease.
